Jesse — thanks for the clear asks. Putting options on the table so procurement has something concrete to evaluate. Quick summary up front: we recommend an annual committed spend with quarterly true-up as the default for predictability, but we can also support monthly true-ups for enterprise customers who need tighter monthly reconciliation.

Options (per-token and simplified rounding):

1) Standard 12-month commit (recommended)
- Commit: 300M tokens / month (annual billing commitment)
- Price: $0.0008 / token on committed usage
- Overage (monthly on-demand beyond commit): 1.6x Redwood on-demand list price -> effective $0.00128 / token
- Burst: up to +40% of monthly commit allowed without higher administrative approvals; beyond that requires pre-approved burst credits or temporary top-up.
- True-up: quarterly true-up (applies unused credits forward; if shortfall at quarter end, invoice difference).

2) Higher commit (discounted)
- Commit: 600M tokens / month
- Price: $0.00065 / token committed
- Overage: 1.35x on-demand -> $0.0008775 / token
- Burst: up to +60% for short windows; negotiated SLA for prolonged sustained bursts.
- True-up: quarterly or annual (customer choice).

3) No-commit / on-demand (for pilot)
- No minimum; list price $0.002 / token; automatic throttling if sustained >20M tokens/day without advance notice; optional short-term burst package available at 1.25x list for single-month surges.

Notes / redlines we typically expect from procurement:
- Clawback / lookback: customers sometimes push for annual true-up only (no monthly billing adjustments). We can accommodate annual true-up if the commit is large enough, but that moves pricing up ~5-8% to account for financial risk.
- Minimum monthly spend: for multi-tier pricing we convert to a dollar-equivalent floor (e.g., $240k/mo for 300M tokens at $0.0008) to keep invoicing simple.

I've attached a one-page matrix (Redwood-Overage-Matrix.xlsx) and a quote (RWI-Quote-Acme-20260501.pdf). If these options look reasonable I can have Marissa or Karthik work with your procurement/legal to draft the SOW language for the commit and overage clauses.

Cheers,

Looping in pricing/legal notes. Per our standard playbook and risk profile for enterprise pilots I recommend we offer two contract templates to present:

A) Quarterly true-up template (lower committed price) — key bullets:
- Quarterly true-up with roll-forward of unused committed tokens for up to 2 quarters.
- Overage = on-demand list * 1.6; invoice monthly for any overage in that month.
- Minimum monthly dollar floor = 60% of monthly commit (applies to monthly invoice).
- Burst: allow 40% short burst; anything sustained >30 days requires notice and will be charged at a negotiated temporary uplift.

B) Annual true-up / no-monthly-adjustments (higher price; for larger customers) — key bullets:
- Annual true-up only (no mid-year invoicing for shortfalls).
- Overage rate exits but applied at year-end true-up (if applicable) at 1.4x on-demand.
- Must commit to at least 80% of annualized volume year-to-year (to limit churn).

Karthik — do you agree with the burst definitions below from engineering? See inline.

Marissa / Priyom — engineering pricing ops input on burst and enforcement semantics. Condensed technical bullets to include in SOW: 

- Burst allowance is measured per-calendar-month as peak additional tokens above committed monthly baseline. Short bursts (<72 hours) are explicitly excluded from "sustained bursts" and will not trigger administrative review as long as aggregate monthly overage < 40% of commit.
- Sustained burst = continuous >= 72 hours AND average daily over-commitment > 20% for a rolling 7-day window. Sustained bursts beyond the approved allowance require a temporary capacity reservation (charged at negotiated uplift) or throttling per our fair-use policy.
- True-up calculations: we use billed tokens (post-prefix-caching adjustments) aggregated by calendar quarter by default. We can switch to rolling-90-days calculation if Acme insists, but this adds reconciliation complexity for us and moves pricing up ~3%.
- Clawback: we avoid retrospective clawbacks other than invoiced shortfalls at agreed true-up cadence. If customer wants no mid-year billing, use annual true-up template and commit to higher floor.

If this looks good I can ask Legal to produce clean SOW language for both template A (quarterly) and B (annual) tomorrow. Priyom — please confirm which template Jesse prefers and I'll circulate.

Thanks,
Karthik
Head of Revenue Pricing | Redwood Inference
